newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany must save more to meet EMU criteria - Buba.
newsitem.headline: Germany must save more to meet EMU criteria - Buba.

text.p: German state and regional governments must save more so that the nation will meet the entry criteria in order to join Europe's planned currency union in 1999, the Bundesbank said on Tuesday.

"In order to avoid running the risk of exceeding the Maastricht Treaty criteria next year, it is imperative to work on making sure that budgets are not exceeded," the Bundesbank said in its December report.

Nations must present 1997 economic data to show their budget deficits do not significantly exceed the Maastricht Treaty reference value of three percent of total gross domestic product to be among the first nations to join the union.
For government debt the reference value is at 60 percent.
The currency union is slated to begin on January 1, 1999, with as many of the 15 European member nations that qualify.
And more important, it will be necessary to ensure that the consolidation efforts will be durable and that more progress can be achieved in the longer term, the Bundesbank said.
"The reduction of deficits is absolutely imperative in order to improve the framework for economic activity," the Bundesbank warned.
For 1996 savings measures will not be enough to prevent the deficit from exceeding last year's levels, already far above the Maastricht Treaty reference levels, the Bundesbank said.
It quoted the Bonn finance ministry's prediction that the deficit ratio to the gross domestic product will likely be around 3.75 percent, but declined to give its own prediction.
The government debt, according to Bonn's predictions, will be near the Maastricht Treaty's 60 percent reference value, or just slightly above it, the Bundesbank said.
In the third quarter the German government's deficit stood at 19.5 billion marks, compared with 14.5 billion marks in the same period a year earlier.
The key reason for the rise is that tax income dipped, the Bundesbank said.
Looking ahead, the Bundesbank said current budget plans show federal, state and local governments envision only a slight increase in spending which should help reduce the deficit.
German states, for example, plan to cut their deficits significantly from the expected deficit of 40 billion marks for 1996.
Even though tax revenues will likely be lower in 1997, after being forecast to be one percent lower this year than in 1995, the Bundesbank said this had been taken into account.
Yet the Bundesbank said there would still be uncertainties and risks entailed in next year's budget developments.
In the third quarter the federal government, states and communities posted a cash deficit of around 30 billion marks, five billion marks above the year-ago level.
The Bundesbank said that income tax income was particularly weak in the third quarter.
